🎙 Iran ready for diplomacy, economic blockade and military confrontation: Deputy FM

📌 Tehran, IRNA - Iran’s deputy foreign minister for legal and international affairs, Kazem Gharibabadi, says the Islamic Republic is ready for three possible scenarios in dealing with the United States: diplomacy, economic blockade, and military aggression.

“The US has shown its bad faith at least three times over the past year and a half. This shows that the US cannot be trusted at the diplomacy table,” Gharibabadi said in a televised interview on Sunday evening.
​
He cited three instances: the 12-day war, which happened while negotiations were underway; the 40-day war, which also took place while talks were underway; and the Islamabad negotiations and the Memorandum of Understanding, which he said lasted at most two weeks.
​
No Iranian requirement removable from any deal
​
Gharibabadi said Iran’s key demands for a deal with the United States include a permanent end to the war on all fronts, an end to the US-imposed economic blockade, the issue of Iran’s blocked assets, and the lifting of certain sanctions, including in the oil sector.
​
He added that the US, after abandoning its commitments and fully annulling the Islamabad understanding, imposed new sanctions whose status must also be resolved, saying these cannot remain a new tool in Washington’s hands requiring Iran to negotiate their removal again.
​
Military presence, implementation timeline
​
Referring to the recent US military presence in the region and the timeline for implementing commitments, Gharibabadi said new military equipment and forces the US added to the region after the previous understanding are among the issues whose status must be clarified, and Washington must take practical steps on them.
​
He said these steps are not time-consuming: Iran’s initial plan to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz was seven days, which over roughly the past two months of consultations with mediators, particularly Qatar and Pakistan, was reduced to two days.
​
This means the measures could be carried out within two days and ultimately lead to the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, and the plan is now on the table, he added.
​
Gaps remain before talks
​
Gharibabadi said that given the Americans’ positions on these issues, there is still a gap before Iran can sit at the negotiating table and finalize the text of an agreement, because the US has views on implementing some of these measures within the two-day window or under the seven-day plan, and ultimately wants to postpone implementation of some of them to other times.
​
“These proposals are not operational from our perspective, because if even one of those issues I mentioned is not implemented at the current stage, fundamentally no understanding can be reached. Even if an understanding is formed, it would be unstable,” he said.
​
“We did not start the war. The Islamic Republic of Iran has fundamentally not been warmongering, and it was not us who started a war with the US or targeted US interests and bases. The war happened and we defended ourselves. We have always been in a position of self-defense.”
​
Iran still in a state of war
​
Gharibabadi said Iran faces two situations: the diplomatic path and the continuation of military threats and war conditions. Some refer to this as “neither war nor peace,” but “my personal belief is that from a legal perspective, we are still in a state of war and not in a neither-war-nor-peace situation.”
​
He said that if the US believes it can achieve results through military aggression, it has tested that path before, but did not achieve the result it expected and . . .

Crypto Idea

Recently, Nvidia plunged by double digits at one point, dragging the entire tech sector down with it. But the market started recovering fairly quickly. Nvidia regained most of its losses, while the S&P 500 and Nasdaq also stabilized.

Now, here's the big question. Why didn't crypto bounce back alongside the stock market? Instead, it kept falling, with Bitcoin eventually dropping to around $68,000.

Here's the hypothesis.

Recently, Binance was hacked, resulting in losses of approximately $6.3 billion. The exchange said it would fully reimburse the losses using its own funds. And we know for a fact that 7,500 BTC, worth approximately $580 million, were withdrawn from Binance's insurance fund afterward. Where exactly those coins went and whether they were sold on the market remains publicly unknown.

But it's entirely possible that Binance has been selling some of its own crypto holdings over the past few days to raise liquidity and cover the massive shortfall caused by the hack. And the panic surrounding Nvidia may have simply created the perfect backdrop for those sales to go largely unnoticed amid a broader market sell-off.

And there's one very important detail here. On November 12, Binance announced that the recovery of assets following the hack was complete.

If hypothesis is even partially correct, Bitcoin's current decline may have less to do with investors suddenly losing faith in crypto and more to do with the emergence of a massive forced seller.

And forced sellers are different from sellers in a typical bear market in one important way. Sooner or later, they run out of assets to sell.

That's why the next few days will be particularly interesting. If the selling pressure really did come from Binance and most of the necessary selling is already behind us, crypto could soon reveal just how strong the underlying demand was beneath all this selling pressure.
